claims.text: The market system is a way of organising an economy in which buyers and sellers interact in markets, and the prices emerging from that interaction decide how scarce resources are allocated.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Market equilibrium is the price at which the quantity buyers plan to buy equals the quantity sellers plan to sell; at a lower price a shortage tends to appear, and at a higher price a surplus tends to appear, which is market disequilibrium.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A minimum price is a legal floor that sellers may not charge below, and a maximum price is a legal ceiling that sellers may not charge above; the legal direction, not the level, decides which a limit is. A minimum price changes the market outcome when set above the equilibrium price, where it tends to leave a surplus because sellers plan to sell more than buyers plan to buy; a maximum price changes it when set below the equilibrium price, where it tends to leave a shortage because buyers plan to buy more than sellers plan to sell. A ceiling set above equilibrium, or a floor set below it, leaves the market price unchanged.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A market system tends to direct resources towards the goods buyers want most, because rising prices reward producers who supply them; it may direct them poorly where buyers cannot be charged for a good or where the price ignores costs imposed on others, so its success depends on the good in question.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The key resources allocation decisions are the three questions every economy must answer because of scarcity: what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom to produce it.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Each of the three allocation decisions constrains the others, because the decision about what to produce shapes which production methods are possible, and the combined cost of those methods limits how much can be offered to consumers.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: An economy answers the three allocation decisions in some way whichever system it uses: a market economy answers them through prices and spending, while an economy run by central officials answers them through government plans.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The price mechanism is the way changing prices act as signals of scarcity and as incentives, moving resources between competing uses without any central planner directing them.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A rising price signals that a good has become scarcer relative to wants, rewards producers with more revenue per unit, and tends to reallocate resources towards the good, because producers expand where the reward is greatest and some buyers step back.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The price mechanism answers the three allocation decisions by steering resources: profit opportunities signal what to produce, the cost of inputs shapes how to produce, and the prices consumers can pay shape for whom to produce.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
